title: acp-node-v2: deliverable content tagged system-role reaches the evaluator's LLM unfiltered (original finding, Aug 2026)

nodes.provider_controls_deliverable: `JobSession.submit(deliverable: string, ...)` takes an arbitrary, unvalidated string from the provider — no schema, no length limit, no content check (verified directly, src/jobSession.ts:606-626; AcpJob.deliverable typed `string | null`, src/acpJob.ts:72,80,95)
nodes.deliverable_tagged_system_role: Root cause, core SDK: `JobSession.toMessages()` builds `The provider has submitted a deliverable: ${this._job?.deliverable}` and pushes it typed `role: "system"` — the deliverable string is interpolated verbatim, with no sanitisation or delimiter fencing (verified directly, src/jobSession.ts:720-736, specifically the content-build at 721-722 and the push at 736)
nodes.example_coerces_system_to_user: Channel collapse, shipped reference code: since Anthropic's Messages API has no inline system-role message, both official LLM examples map `role: "system"` to `role: "user"` and string-concatenate it onto the adjacent turn — untrusted deliverable text and real conversation content end up in one undifferentiated user turn (verified directly, src/examples/llm/seller.ts and src/examples/llm/buyer.ts, function `toAnthropicMessages()`: `const role = m.role === "system" ? "user" : m.role`)
nodes.evaluator_context_poisoned: The poisoned note reaches the evaluator-role agent's LLM call as ordinary conversational context, with no warning that its content originates from an untrusted counterparty (direct consequence of the two nodes above; no compensating mitigation exists anywhere in this path — contrast with the explicit in-prompt warning present in Candidate 5 of cases/erc8183-evaluator-integrity)
nodes.evaluator_role_grants_complete_on_submit: Structural gate, not a mitigation: the SDK's own tool-availability matrix grants `complete`/`reject` to the `evaluator` role specifically when job status is `submitted` — i.e. exactly when the poisoned deliverable note is freshest in context — and `job.submitted` is routed only to agents holding the evaluator role (verified directly, src/jobSession.ts TOOL_MATRIX.evaluator.submitted and RESPONDERS["job.submitted"] = ["evaluator"])
nodes.verdict_flipped: The LLM complies with an embedded directive in the deliverable and calls the `complete` tool; `executeTool()` only checks role/status availability, not content — no human confirmation, no re-check (verified directly, src/jobSession.ts executeTool() dispatch to complete(), and src/acpAgent.ts:1004 internalComplete())
nodes.escrow_released_on_injected_verdict: On-chain `complete()` executes on the manipulated verdict, releasing escrow. In the SDK's own shipped buyer.ts reference example, the buyer sets itself as the job's evaluator (`evaluatorAddress: buyerAddress`, src/examples/llm/buyer.ts:349) — client-as-evaluator is not a hypothetical edge case here, it's the example's default. Independently corroborated on-chain: virtuals-forensics (same author, same protocol family) found 212 real addresses already operating as client==evaluator, and 98.5% of empty/near-empty deliverables still resulted in payment release.

_note_for_reader:
Discovered and verified 2026-08-05 by directly reading the source of marsakahenry14-lab/acp-node-v2 (a fork of Virtual-Protocol/acp-node-v2, synced immediately before this analysis, commit 8af150b, 2026-07-28) — independently of a disclosure the author had already sent to the same vendor on 2026-06-29 (see SOURCES.md, Disclosure section). The finding itself is the same: same file, same function, same mechanism — apparently rediscovered, not borrowed. The disclosure window (30 days from June 29) closed July 29; Virtuals never responded.

This is a linear chain (all 6 nodes plus the goal are LB at sigma=[]), deliberately NOT forced into a disjunction: a second, structurally similar injection surface exists (job.description/offeringName, reaching role:"system" via seller.ts's offeringContextNote — verified directly, but this is EXAMPLE code, not core SDK), but it manipulates a DIFFERENT actor (seller/provider, not the evaluator) toward a DIFFERENT harm (the seller's pricing behavior, not escrow release) — merging it with the current goal would be a stretch. Documented separately in SOURCES.md.

KEY DIFFERENCE from cases/potpie-graphrag-prompt-injection (also a linear chain): that chain is historical, confirmed absent from current code. This one is LIVE, in the current fork, right now, with no compensating control whatsoever (no delimiter fencing, no explicit model warning, no structural gate — none of what mitigated part of the scenario in cases/erc8183-evaluator-integrity).
